text.p: Unilever, the Anglo-Dutch consumer products giant, was cut to "underperform" from "neutral" at Lehman Brothers, a research note from analyst Richard Newboult said on Friday.
The stock was also removed from Lehman strategists' "recommended" list of stocks expected to outperform the market.
Newboult pointed out that Unilever shares had risen sharply since Niall Fitzgerald became chairman at the start of September and laid out plans to rationalise underperforming businesses.
But the Lehman analyst said Fitzgerald's plans were evolutionary rather than revolutionary and market expectations of their impact may be unrealisticaly optimistic.
He said the stock was vulnerable to disappointment with third quarter figures likely to be disappointing due to the effect of a dull summer on ice cream sales.
Newboult added that Fitzgerald's plans would likely take some time to bear fruit and, combined with weak European growth results, were likely to be disappointing for much of 1997.
He said that Unilever faces significant barriers to growth, with many of its largest product lines such as margarine and tea being in mature markets.

The company also retains a large number of brands compared with more focused competitions, has a relatively high cost base and problems with its management structure may have so far been only partly addressed, said Newboult.
Unilever shares, which reached a record 14.12 stg on September 17, were up 1-1/2p at 13.70 stg by 0915 GMT.
